content: The lotus effect, as observed in material science, refers to the remarkable superhydrophobic and self-cleaning properties of lotus plant leaves. In certain Eastern cultures, the lotus plant symbolizes purity. Despite thriving in muddy rivers and lakes, the leaves and flowers of the lotus remain clean. Botanists studying these leaves have discovered a natural cleaning mechanism inherent to their structure. This phenomenon was first identified by Wilhelm Barthlott in 1982, who also holds a patent related to this discovery. The microscopic structure and surface chemistry of lotus leaves prevent them from being wetted by liquids with a contact angle greater than 90° on an unstructured surface of the same material. With water contact angles reaching up to 170°, water droplets roll off the surface of the leaves like mercury, carrying away dirt, small insects, and other contaminants. This property is termed superhydrophobicity, commonly referred to as the lotus effect. Similar behavior is observed in water droplets on taro and nasturtium leaves. Nanotechnologists have developed treatments, coatings, paints, roof tiles, fabrics, and other surfaces that mimic the lotus leaf's ability to remain dry and self-cleaning. These effects are typically achieved using specialized fluorochemical or silicone treatments on structured surfaces or compositions containing micro-scale particulates. Superhydrophobic coatings incorporating Teflon™ microparticles have been utilized on medical diagnostic slides for over 30 years. Such effects can also be achieved by combining polyethylene glycol with glucose and sucrose (or other insoluble particulates) alongside a hydrophobic substance. One method involves making an aluminum surface superhydrophobic by immersing it in sodium hydroxide for several hours, which roughens the surface, followed by spin-coating a 2-nanometer-thick layer of perfluorononane. This process increases the water contact angle from 67° to 168°, an effect explained by Cassie's law. Electron microscopy reveals that the treated aluminum surface resembles the porous microstructure of a lotus leaf, containing trapped air. Any surface treatment that creates microor nano-scale roughness with features having a height-to-width ratio greater than one, subsequently coated with a thin hydrophobic layer, will exhibit the lotus effect. In commercial applications, water-repellent clothing has been developed and marketed by brands like Gap and Dockers, using a fabric called Nano-Care. Water-repellent glass panels are also available for use on conservatory roofs. Stocoat Lotusan is an exterior coating (paint) that mimics the microstructure of the lotus leaf surface, achieving similar water-repellent and self-cleaning properties, collectively termed the Lotus Effect. Water does not adhere to the surface but rolls off, carrying debris away in the process. By remaining dry, the coating resists mold, mildew, and algae. Despite being hydrophobic, the coating is highly permeable to water vapor. Superhydrophobic coatings with the lotus effect, when applied to microwave antennas, can significantly reduce rain fade and prevent the accumulation of ice and snow.
